changes._why: the inner join dropped a staff member who handled no rental, though the request counts each
request: Count the rentals each staff member handled, by `rental.staff_id`.
Show each staff member's `staff_id` and `first_name` with the count, `0` for one who handled none, ordered by `staff_id`.
changes.sql:
SELECT s.staff_id, s.first_name, s.last_name, s.address_id, s.email, s.store_id, s.active, s.username, s.password, s.last_update, COUNT(r.rental_id) AS rentals -- every column but picture, a BLOB which does not print
FROM staff s
         LEFT JOIN rental r ON r.staff_id = s.staff_id
GROUP BY s.staff_id

changes._why: the inner joins dropped a staff member with no rental
request: A staff member works at one store, but may rent out a copy of another store.
For each staff member, count the rentals they handled whose copy is at their own store, and those whose copy is elsewhere, with `CASE` inside `SUM`; a staff member with no rental shows two zeros.
Show the `staff_id`, `first_name`, `store_id` and the two counts, ordered by `staff_id`.
changes.sql:
SELECT s.staff_id, s.first_name, s.last_name, s.address_id, s.email, s.store_id, s.active, s.username, s.password, s.last_update, -- every column but picture, a BLOB which does not print
       SUM(CASE WHEN i.store_id = s.store_id THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS own_store,
       SUM(CASE WHEN i.store_id <> s.store_id THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS other_store
FROM staff s
         LEFT JOIN rental r ON r.staff_id = s.staff_id
         LEFT JOIN inventory i ON i.inventory_id = r.inventory_id
GROUP BY s.staff_id
ORDER BY s.staff_id

changes._why: the title asks whether, but the SQL never compared the two cities, and city names repeat across countries
request: The view's `city` and `country` are where the staff member lives, and `SID` is the store they work at.

Join each row to its store, the store's address, city and country, and show the `ID`, `name`, where they live, where they work, and whether the two are the same city of the same country, ordered by `ID`.
City names repeat across countries, so the comparison takes the country too.
changes.sql:
SELECT l.*,
       ci.city                                        AS store_city,
       co.country                                     AS store_country,
       (l.city = ci.city AND l.country = co.country) AS lives_in_store_city
FROM staff_list l
         JOIN store st ON st.store_id = l.SID
         JOIN address a ON a.address_id = st.address_id
         JOIN city ci ON ci.city_id = a.city_id
         JOIN country co ON co.country_id = ci.country_id
ORDER BY l.ID

changes._why: no ORDER BY, so the order of the groups was unspecified
request: Every customer has an `email`; SAKILA_CUSTOMER_B_06 checks it.
Take the part after the `@` as the domain, group the customers by it, and show each domain with the number of its customers, the most first; domains with the same number are ordered by name.
The group is by an expression, not by a column.
changes.sql:
SELECT SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1) AS domain, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customer
GROUP BY domain
ORDER BY customers DESC, domain

changes._why: the inner join dropped a store with no copy, though the request counts each store
request: For each store, a store without a copy included, count the distinct films it has at least one copy of, and, of those, the films no other store has a copy of.
Show the `store_id` and both counts, ordered by `store_id`.
The second count needs a correlated condition on the inventory of the other stores.
changes.sql:
SELECT st.*,
       COUNT(DISTINCT i.film_id)                  AS films,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
                          WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                                           FROM inventory o
                                           WHERE o.film_id = i.film_id
                                             AND o.store_id <> st.store_id)
                              THEN i.film_id END) AS films_only_here
FROM store st
         LEFT JOIN inventory i ON i.store_id = st.store_id
GROUP BY st.store_id
ORDER BY st.store_id

changes._why: city names repeat (across countries), so ordering by the name alone does not fix the order of the rows
request: Find the cities whose name starts with the letter `Q`.
Show the whole rows, ordered by the name, then by `city_id`; names repeat across countries.
A `LIKE` with a trailing wildcard.

FROM city
WHERE city LIKE 'Q%'
ORDER BY city, city_id

changes._why: two cities may share the name and the count; city_id breaks the tie
request: Count the addresses of each city, and keep the cities with more than one.
Show the `city_id`, the `city` and the count, the most first; cities with the same count are ordered by the name, then by `city_id`.
changes.sql:
SELECT ci.*, COUNT(*) AS addresses
FROM city ci
         JOIN address a ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
GROUP BY ci.city_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY addresses DESC, ci.city, ci.city_id

changes._why: STAFF_LIST has no Advanced exercise; the view's home country against the rental-to-customer path
changes.title: the staff members who served a customer living outside their own country
changes.file_header: Exercises at the advanced level on staff_list: a correlated EXISTS across the rentals, customers and their addresses. Each poses a question, answers it, and shows what the installed data gives back.
request: Find the staff members who handled at least one rental for a customer who lives in another country than the staff member does, as the view says.
Show their `ID`, `name` and `country`, ordered by `ID`.
A correlated `EXISTS` walks from the staff member's rentals to the customers' countries.
changes.sql:
SELECT l.ID, l.name, l.country
FROM staff_list l
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM rental r
                       JOIN customer cu ON cu.customer_id = r.customer_id
                       JOIN address a ON a.address_id = cu.address_id
                       JOIN city ci ON ci.city_id = a.city_id
                       JOIN country co ON co.country_id = ci.country_id
              WHERE r.staff_id = l.ID
                AND co.country <> l.country)
ORDER BY l.ID

changes._why: email is nullable, and SAKILA_CUSTOMER_B_03 takes the domain after the @ of every one
changes.title: the customers whose email is missing or not one address
request: SAKILA_CUSTOMER_B_03 takes the part of each `email` after the `@`, which `email`, nullable, does not promise.

Find the customers whose `email` is `NULL`, holds a space, or does not have exactly one `@` with something on both sides; show their `customer_id`, names and `email`, ordered by `customer_id`; the check passes when nothing comes back.
changes.sql:
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, email
FROM customer
WHERE email IS NULL
   OR email NOT LIKE '_%@_%'
   OR CHAR_LENGTH(email) - CHAR_LENGTH(REPLACE(email, '@', '')) <> 1
   OR email REGEXP '[[:space:]]'
ORDER BY customer_id

changes._why: the spending exercises join payment with inner joins, assuming every customer has paid
changes.title: the customers with no payment
request: The exercises on what customers spent join `payment` with inner joins, which drops a customer who never paid.
Find the customers with no payment: their `customer_id` and names, ordered by `customer_id`; the check passes when nothing comes back.
changes.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name
FROM customer c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payment p WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id)
ORDER BY c.customer_id

changes._why: film.rental_duration against the rental dates is the schema's own notion of lateness (get_customer_balance), and no exercise uses it per customer
changes.title: the five customers who returned late most often
request: A rental is late when it was returned more days after it was rented than its film's `rental_duration`, as `get_customer_balance` counts it.
Show the five customers with the most late returns, with their counts, the most first; ties are ordered by `customer_id`.
A rental not yet returned has no `return_date`, so it drops out of the comparison.
changes.sql:
SELECT c.*, COUNT(*) AS late_returns
FROM customer c
         JOIN rental r ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id
         JOIN inventory i ON i.inventory_id = r.inventory_id
         JOIN film f ON f.film_id = i.film_id
WHERE DATEDIFF(r.return_date, r.rental_date) > f.rental_duration
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY late_returns DESC, c.customer_id
LIMIT 5

changes._why: no exercise uses LAG over dates, which rental_date makes natural
changes.title: the five customers with the longest gap between two rentals
request: For each customer, take the days between each rental and the customer's previous one, and keep the longest.
Show the five customers with the longest gap, with the gap in days, the longest first; ties are ordered by `customer_id`.
`LAG` gives each rental the one before it; `rental_id` breaks a tie of `rental_date`, which is not unique per customer.
changes.sql:
WITH gaps AS (SELECT r.customer_id,
                     DATEDIFF(r.rental_date,
                              LAG(r.rental_date) OVER (PARTITION BY r.customer_id ORDER BY r.rental_date, r.rental_id)) AS gap_days
              FROM rental r)
SELECT c.*, MAX(g.gap_days) AS longest_gap
FROM customer c
         JOIN gaps g ON g.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY longest_gap DESC, c.customer_id
LIMIT 5

changes._why: SAKILA_COUNTRY_B_02 says the names are unique and the A tier orders by them, but country.country has no unique key
changes.title: the country names found more than once
request: SAKILA_COUNTRY_B_02 relies on the country names being unique, and the Advanced exercises order by them; the schema does not make them unique.
Find the names that more than one row of `country` has, with how many, ordered by the name; the check passes when nothing comes back.

FROM country
GROUP BY country
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY country

changes._why: city names identify a city within its country in several exercises, which no key enforces
changes.title: the city names found more than once in a country
request: Some exercises name a city by its country and its name, which no key of `city` makes unique.
Find each `country_id` and city name that more than one city has, with how many, ordered by `country_id` and the name; the check passes when nothing comes back.

FROM city

changes._why: postal_code is nullable, and no exercise shows that a missing one takes two forms, nor that = '' is not true for NULL
changes.title: how many addresses have no postal code, as NULL and as an empty string
request: A missing `postal_code` may be `NULL` or the empty string.
Count the addresses whose `postal_code` is `NULL`, and, apart, those whose `postal_code` is the empty string, in one row.
`postal_code = ''` is not true for a `NULL`; in MySQL a condition sums as `1` or `0`.
changes.sql:
SELECT SUM(postal_code IS NULL) AS null_postal_codes,
       SUM(postal_code = '')    AS empty_postal_codes
FROM address
